tagline: Teardrop island of tea and elephants
overview:
Sri Lanka is a pear-shaped island in the Indian Ocean, just off the southeastern tip of India across a shallow strait dotted with sandbanks. It covers about 65,600 km², roughly the size of West Virginia, and packs beaches, rainforest, dry plains and misty mountains into a short drive.

About 22 million people live in Sri Lanka. Sinhala and Tamil are both official languages, and English is widely used. Colombo on the west coast is the commercial capital and largest city; the country's parliament sits in the nearby planned city of Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte.

Sri Lanka is a republic with an elected president and parliament. It is famous for Ceylon tea grown on cool highland slopes, for cinnamon and sapphires, for cricket, and for ancient Buddhist cities where enormous brick stupas and carved reservoirs have stood for 2,000 years.
landAndNature: A central massif of mountains rises to Pidurutalagala at 2,524 meters, catching two monsoons, one from the southwest between May and September and one from the northeast from December to February, which is why one side of the island can be soaking while the other is dry. Tea bushes cover the cool slopes, and rainforest survives in Sinharaja reserve, home to birds found nowhere else. The dry northern plains hold ancient irrigation tanks, giant reservoirs built by kings more than a thousand years ago and still watering fields. Sri Lanka has about 6,000 wild elephants, leopards in Yala park, sloth bears and the largest gatherings of wild Asian elephants anywhere. Blue whales, the biggest animals ever, feed off the southern coast.
peopleAndCulture: Most Sri Lankans are Sinhalese and mainly Buddhist, with Tamil communities who are largely Hindu, plus Muslim and Christian populations, so temples, kovils, mosques and churches often stand within a few streets. Rice and curry means a plate of rice ringed by half a dozen dishes: dhal, coconut sambol pounded with chili, jackfruit, fish. Hoppers, bowl-shaped pancakes cooked in a small pan, are a breakfast favorite. Cricket is the national passion, and Sri Lanka won the World Cup in 1996. The Kandy Esala Perahera parades decorated elephants, dancers and drummers by torchlight for days each summer. Stilt fishermen on the south coast perch on poles planted in the surf.
history: Sinhalese settlers arrived from northern India around 500 BC, and Buddhism came in the 200s BC; the ancient capitals of Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa built vast stupas, monasteries and reservoirs. Tamil kingdoms and invasions from southern India shaped the north. Portugal took coastal areas in the 1500s, the Dutch followed, and Britain seized the whole island by 1815, renaming it Ceylon and covering the highlands with tea after a disease destroyed the coffee crop. Independence came on February 4, 1948, and the country took the name Sri Lanka in 1972. From 1983 to 2009 a civil war was fought between the government and the Tamil Tigers, who sought a separate state in the north and east; tens of thousands died before the war ended. In 2004 the Indian Ocean tsunami killed more than 30,000 people here.
funFacts: Sri Lanka was the world's first country to elect a woman prime minister, Sirimavo Bandaranaike, in 1960.
Sigiriya is a palace and fortress built atop a 200-meter rock column, reached by stairs past 1,500-year-old wall paintings.
The country supplies most of the world's true cinnamon, peeled as thin bark and rolled into quills by hand.
Sri Lanka's flag includes a lion with a sword plus stripes representing its Tamil and Muslim communities.
Adam's Peak has a footprint-shaped mark at its summit revered by Buddhists, Hindus, Muslims and Christians alike.
